svg.text: Testing a claim: it cured my sister is not evidence
The same standard applies to a plant and to a tablet
Why a testimonial convinces, and misleads
Most illnesses get better on their own
Symptoms come and go; people buy at the worst point
Expectation itself relieves pain and nausea
The hospital treatment is often taken at the same time
Those it failed do not appear on the radio
Every one of these produces a true story
about a treatment that did nothing
The people it did not help are missing from the count
What would count as evidence
A comparison group who did not get it
Allocation by chance, so the groups start alike
An outcome measured, not remembered
Everyone enrolled counted at the end
Published, so others can check it
Only a comparison can separate the treatment
from what would have happened anyway
Only randomisation shows cause
Plants have given medicine some of its best drugs
Artemisinin for malaria, quinine from cinchona bark, morphine from the poppy, digoxin from foxglove, aspirin from willow
In each case the active compound was identified, purified, measured into a known dose and tested against a comparison
The plant was the starting point. The testing is what made it a medicine.
What a nurse says when asked whether a remedy works
Not: it is all superstition. Not: yes, try it. Both answers end the conversation and neither is honest.
Say what is known, say what is not known, say what the specific risk is, and keep the door open.
A patient who trusts your honesty will tell you when she starts something new.
